slides.body: Google turned on a feature that lets its AI read every email in your inbox. Bank statements, medical letters, tax filings, all scanned by default with no warning

slides.headline: GOOGLE BURIED A SECOND OFF SWITCH IN A DIFFERENT MENU
slides.body: There's a visible switch called Smart features and personalization and a second one buried under Manage Workspace smart feature settings. You need both off or nothing changes

slides.headline: YOUR PHONE DIDN'T GET THE MESSAGE
slides.body: You turned everything off on your laptop. Google's AI kept reading through the Gmail app in your pocket because phone settings don't sync with desktop

slides.body: If you've used Google's Gemini chatbot, those conversations can be reviewed by actual humans at Google. Delete them at myactivity.google.com/product/gemini and move sensitive emails to Proton Mail

slides.headline: EVERY CLIENT EMAIL IN YOUR GMAIL IS BEING READ BY GOOGLE'S AI RIGHT NOW
slides.body: Your contracts, your client conversations, your invoices, all sitting in an inbox that Google's AI reads by default. Most business owners have no idea this is happening to their clients' data

slides.headline: FOLLOW NOW OR THIS PAGE DISAPPEARS FROM YOUR FEED FOREVER
slides.body: Send this to the friend who still thinks they turned Google's email scanning off

caption:
Swipe to see the two hidden switches that control whether Google's AI reads your Gmail 📧

Google turned on AI email scanning across every Gmail account by default, reading bank statements, tax files, medical letters, every attachment. The main off switch is under Settings → Smart features and personalization, but a second hidden switch lives under Manage Workspace smart feature settings and both must be turned off. Phone settings don't sync with desktop so you have to turn it off separately in the Gmail app. Gemini chat history may be reviewed by actual humans at Google, delete it at myactivity.google.com/product/gemini. A class-action lawsuit is forming and users are migrating sensitive emails to Proton Mail.

When a company hides the real privacy switch behind a decoy, it's not a design flaw. The 8.1 million people who saw this can't unsee it.
